messages.author: 3e3ca0351e8e43f2
messages.subject: Re: Variance from detection probability
parts:
Dear Steve,

Many thanks for your rapid reply and for the primate paper.

I suspect that you have identified the problem correctly and that our =
survey
teams are not always estimating the distance accurately. Some comments:

1. Transects (26 in each year 2009 and 2010) are placed randomly =
(systematic
segmented parallel line) and are not on paths.

2. Almost all measurements are taken with laser range-finders (only when
range-finders break do we resort to tape measures). Compasses are used =
to
find angles, although these were taken less accurately in 2009: =
obviously a
particular problem when observations are close to the line.

3. We are only finding this problem with wild pigs and not with other
species such as deer or primates (the latter are also found in large
groups).

4. I suspect that fast-moving wild pigs, which are often partially and
temporarily hidden by long grass and vegetation, may be harder to locate =
and
thus estimate distance to than primates, even if both are found in large
groups. Positions of primates on first detection may be easier to record =
as
individual trees may be more distinctive. This could explain why =
detection
is somewhat confused for pigs and distances have been under-estimated. A
greater proportion of large groups (10+) of wild pig are recorded at =
zero
distance compared to smaller groups.

Could the problem therefore be linked to a combination of =
under-estimation
of distances as well as fast-moving pigs increasing the difficulties of
accurate distance recording? Has anyone encountered similar issues =
before
between species?

Thanks again

Hugo

-----Original Message-----
From: Steve Buckland [mailto:st...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk]=20
Sent: 17 January 2011 16:33
To: Hugo Rainey
Cc: DISTANCE...@jiscmail.ac.uk
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Variance from detection probability

Hugo, this used to be a very common problem, which we see less often=20
now, both because the message is getting through better that you need=20
accurate distance estimates and because the technology is better and=20
cheaper for measuring distances - e.g. laser rangefinders. =20
Unfortunately, when such a high proportion of detections is recorded as=20
at zero distance, reliable estimation of the detection function is not=20
possible. Note that this problem can also occur if transects are along=20
trails, and the species of interest uses the trails. If you've ruled=20
out that possibility (solution is to place transects randomly; if you=20
have to cut transects, do a minimum cut, so as not to create obvious=20
trails), and are confident that this is a measurement issue, then it can =

only be resolved by training of the observers. In your current=20
analyses, you are likely to be overestimating densities, because you're=20
trying to fit a spike in the detection function at zero distance which=20
probably isn't real. That leads you to underestimate the proportion of=20
animals on the strip that you detect and overestimate abundance. The=20
same problem is often encountered in primate surveys. Off the list,=20
I'll send a copy of the following paper, which discusses this issue.

Steve Buckland

Buckland, S.T., Plumptre, A.J., Thomas, L. and Rexstad, E.A. 2010.Design =

and analysis of line transect surveys for primates./International=20
Journal of Primatology/ *31*, 833-847.

messages.author: 395035ddfae29510
messages.subject: Re: Variance from detection probability
parts:
I think this is more likely to be a problem that the pigs are just not =
seen
away from the transect because of dense vegetation and are often seen
crossing the transect ahead of the observer - we have the same problem =
with
duikers seen on transects in forests in Uganda. There's not a lot you =
can do
about it to improve the census - I think you need a different census =
method
for species such as this. We generally census pig dung rather than count
live ones for the same reason.=20

Andy

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Variance from detection probability
parts:
Hugo, a contributory factor if transect lines are cut, or vegetation
trampled along the line, is that, for moving animals, the observers only
see them when they cross the transect, so record zero distance. Again,
with larger groups, if visibility is better along the line, the animals
that are visible may be the ones that are on the line. These issues can
be very difficult if not impossible to resolve.

Steve
